Module 3

The shell: COMMAND.COM and /bin/sh

A shell is the first program most users meet and the last one most students read. This module reads two of them: COMMAND.COM from MS-DOS 4.00, written in 8086 assembly for machines with a few hundred kilobytes of RAM and one running program at a time, and /bin/sh from FreeBSD 15.1, a C program running as an ordinary process on a demand-paged, multitasking kernel. Both read a command, find it, run it and wire up its input and output, but the hardware and kernel underneath push them into very different designs. Module 2 covered the kernel services (INT 21h, handles, EXEC, fork, execve); here we study the user program that strings them together.

MS-DOS 2d04cacFreeBSD release/15.1.045 source listings4 study cases7 exercisesabout 85 min read
Francesco Valerio Buccoli · francesco@buccoli.com

Learning goals. After this module you can:

  • explain how SYSINIT starts COMMAND.COM and how login(1) starts sh, including /P, /E, COMSPEC, AUTOEXEC.BAT, -sh and .profile;
  • describe COMMAND.COM's resident/transient split, find the checksum that decides whether the transient part is reloaded, and explain why sh needs no such split;
  • trace each shell's main loop from prompt to program exit, naming the routines and system calls involved;
  • explain how each shell implements <, > and >>, and why COMMAND.COM edits its own Job File Table while sh uses dup2 and fcntl(F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC);
  • contrast temporary-file pipes with kernel pipes and concurrent processes, step by step, for dir | sort > out.txt;
  • explain why editing a running batch file changes what runs, and how sh parses scripts into trees;
  • compare the DOS environment block with sh variables and environ, and INT 23h with signals, process groups and job control;
  • argue from the source why cd must be a builtin in FreeBSD, and why the reason differs in MS-DOS.

Prerequisites.

  • Module 0 (00-lab.md): the MS-DOS 4.00 floppy image built from this tree (with DEBUG.COM), tools/dos_run.py, and the FreeBSD 15.1 VM with /usr/src, truss, ktrace and dtrace.
  • Module 1 (SYSINIT EXECs the shell; the FreeBSD kernel starts /sbin/init; section 3.1 takes it from there to getty, login and the shell) and Module 2 (INT 21h dispatch, PSP and Job File Table, EXEC vs fork/execve, the memory arena).
  • Reading 8086 assembly: segment registers, segment:offset addresses, REP MOVSB, INT.

3.1 What a shell is, and how each system starts one#

A shell (or command interpreter) is a user program that reads commands from a keyboard or a file and causes them to be carried out. Internal commands (MS-DOS term) or builtins (Unix term) are code inside the shell itself; external commands are program files that the shell finds and asks the kernel to run. Neither kernel treats its shell specially: each runs whatever program it is told to.

MS-DOS 4.00: SYSINIT EXECs COMMAND.COM#

Module 1 ended where SYSINIT, the last stage of the DOS boot, has processed CONFIG.SYS. The default shell is COMMND DB "\COMMAND.COM",0 (SYSINIT2.ASM line 1493) with the argument string COMMAND_LINE DB 2,0,"P" (SYSINIT1.ASM lines 279-280), whose zero byte is replaced by the current switch character (SYSCONF.ASM lines 604-606): the default is \COMMAND.COM /P. A SHELL= line replaces both parts:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.1 – SHELL= overwrites the program name and the default arguments (excerpt) (SYSCONF.ASM lines 2296-2329)Source ↗
TRYS:
        CMP     AH,'S'
        JNZ     TRYX
        MOV     [COMMAND_LINE+1],0
        MOV     DI,OFFSET COMMND + 1
        MOV     [DI-1],AL
STORESHELL:
        CALL    GETCHR
        OR      AL,AL
        JZ      GETSHPARMS
        CMP     AL," "
        JB      ENDSH
        MOV     [DI],AL
        INC     DI
        JMP     STORESHELL
⋮
GETSHPARMS:
        MOV     BYTE PTR [DI],0
        MOV     DI,OFFSET COMMAND_LINE+1
PARMLOOP:
        CALL    GETCHR
        CMP     AL," "
        JB      ENDSH
        MOV     [DI],AL
        INC     DI
        JMP     PARMLOOP

Line 2299 erases the default /P, and only what follows the file name becomes the argument string, so SHELL=C:\DOS\COMMAND.COM without /P starts a shell that is not permanent. SYSINIT then EXECs the shell (INT 21h function 4Bh, Module 2).

COMMAND.COM starts at CONPROC in INIT.ASM and parses its command tail at offset 80h of its Program Segment Prefix (PSP, the 256-byte header DOS builds in front of every program), dispatching on each switch (INIT.ASM lines 512-524):

Switch Handler Effect in the source
/P SetPSwitch PERMCOM; COMMAND becomes its own parent with LODCOM as terminate address, and installs INT 2Eh (lines 838-865); EXIT (INT 21h 4Ch, TCMD2B.ASM) lands back in the same shell
/C string SetSSwitch SINGLECOM points at the rest of the line: run one command, then exit
/E:n SetESwitch environment size in bytes, rounded up to 16-byte paragraphs
/D SetDSwitch skip AUTOEXEC.BAT and the date/time prompt
/F SetFSwitch answer every critical error with Fail

A permanent shell (unless /D is given) allocates a batch segment for AUTOEXEC.BAT and checks that the file opens (lines 1001-1007, 1157-1173); if it does not, the segment is freed and the date and time prompts appear instead (lines 1221-1234). If the parent passed no environment (the PSP field at offset 2Ch is zero, INIT.ASM lines 358-372), the shell uses one assembled into its own image:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.2 – the built-in default environment: an empty PATH and COMSPEC (ENVDATA.ASM lines 11-28)Source ↗
ENVIRONMENT SEGMENT PUBLIC PARA        ; Default COMMAND environment

        PUBLIC  ECOMSPEC,ENVIREND,PATHSTRING

        ORG     0
PATHSTRING DB   "PATH="
USERPATH LABEL  BYTE

        DB      0               ; Null path
        DB      "COMSPEC="
ECOMSPEC DB     "\COMMAND.COM"      ;AC062
        DB      134 DUP (0)

ENVIREND        LABEL   BYTE

ENVIRONSIZ EQU  $-PATHSTRING
ENVIRONSIZ2 EQU $-ECOMSPEC
ENVIRONMENT ENDS

COMSPEC records where COMMAND.COM lives on disk. Section 3.2 shows why the shell needs it.

FreeBSD 15.1: login(1) execs the user's shell#

init starts getty, getty runs login, and login replaces itself with the shell named in the user's password entry or in login.conf (login.c lines 445-453). It marks the shell as a login shell with a convention as old as Unix:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.3 – login(1) prefixes argv[0] with a dash and execs the shell (login.c lines 649-662)Source ↗
        /*
         * Login shells have a leading '-' in front of argv[0]
         */
        p = strrchr(pwd->pw_shell, '/');
        if (asprintf(&arg0, "-%s", p ? p + 1 : pwd->pw_shell) >= MAXPATHLEN) {
                syslog(LOG_ERR, "user: %s: shell exceeds maximum pathname size",
                    username);
                errx(1, "shell exceeds maximum pathname size");
        } else if (arg0 == NULL) {
                err(1, "asprintf()");
        }

        execlp(shell, arg0, (char *)0);
        err(1, "%s", shell);

procargs() treats a leading - in argv[0], or -l, as "login shell" (options.c lines 86-92), and main() acts on it:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.4 – a login shell reads /etc/profile and ~/.profile; an interactive one also reads $ENV (main.c lines 138-155)Source ↗
        if (login) {
                state = 1;
                read_profile("/etc/profile");
state1:
                state = 2;
                if (privileged == 0)
                        read_profile("${HOME-}/.profile");
                else
                        read_profile("/etc/suid_profile");
        }
state2:
        state = 3;
        if (!privileged && iflag) {
                if ((shinit = lookupvar("ENV")) != NULL && *shinit != '\0') {
                        state = 3;
                        read_profile(shinit);
                }
        }

Then cmdloop(1) runs until end of file or exit. A script is run by a new sh process: the kernel's #! image activator starts the interpreter with the script's path as an argument (imgact_shell.c lines 60-84), procargs() opens it as input (options.c lines 106-110), and sh also runs a file that execve rejects with ENOEXEC as a script unless it looks binary (exec.c lines 167-192).

MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Who starts the first shell SYSINIT, after CONFIG.SYS login, after authentication
Choice of shell SHELL=, default \COMMAND.COM pw_shell, or login.conf
"Top-level shell" marker /P (permanent) argv[0] starts with -
Startup script AUTOEXEC.BAT /etc/profile, ~/.profile, then $ENV
One command and exit COMMAND /C string sh -c string
Scripts run by the same COMMAND.COM process a new sh process

3.2 COMMAND.COM's resident and transient portions#

A PC running MS-DOS 4.00 might have 256-640 KB of RAM, and only one program runs at a time. Memory the shell keeps while a program runs is memory the program cannot use, so COMMAND.COM is split into pieces with different lifetimes. The header of COMMAND1.ASM states the design:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.5 – the three-part design of COMMAND.COM (COMMAND1.ASM lines 13-28)Source ↗
; FUNCTION:            This version of COMMAND is divided into three distinct
;                      parts.  First is the resident portion, which includes
;                      handlers for interrupts  23H (Cntrl-C), 24H (fatal
;                      error), and 2EH (command line execute); it also has
;                      code to test and, if necessary, reload the transient
;                      portion. Following the resident is the init code, which
;                      is overwritten after use.  Then comes the transient
;                      portion, which includes all command processing (whether
;                      internal or external).  The transient portion loads at
;                      the end of physical memory, and it may be overlayed by
;                      programs that need as much memory as possible. When the
;                      resident portion of command regains control from a user
;                      program, a check sum is performed on the transient
;                      portion to see if it must be reloaded.  Thus programs
;                      which do not need maximum memory will save the time
;                      required to reload COMMAND when they terminate.

The split is made by segment order. COMSEG.ASM lists the segments in load order and gathers them into two groups (segments addressed through one segment register):

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.6 – the resident group and the transient group (COMSEG.ASM lines 41-42)Source ↗
RESGROUP  GROUP CODERES,DATARES,BATARENA,BATSEG,ENVARENA,ENVIRONMENT,INIT,TAIL
TRANGROUP GROUP TRANCODE,TRANDATA,TRANSPACE,TRANTAIL

RESGROUP holds resident code and data, a batch segment and a default environment for the first shell, the init code, and an empty TAIL segment whose label TRANSTART marks where the transient image begins (COMMAND2.ASM lines 600-608). TRANGROUP holds the transient code, its data (TRANDATA: messages and tables, mostly constant) and its work variables (TRANSPACE). The link step converts the result with exe2bin into a flat .COM image (MAKEFILE lines 132-134) that starts at PROGSTART, offset 100h, which jumps to the init code (COMMAND1.ASM lines 401-411).

INIT places the transient at the top of the memory block DOS gave the shell:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.7 – INIT computes TRNSEG, the transient's segment (INIT.ASM lines 351-357)Source ↗
        MOV     DX,OFFSET TRANGROUP:TRANSPACEEND + 15 ; dx = size of transient
        MOV     CL,4                            ;  in paragraphs.
        SHR     DX,CL
        mov     [trnsize],dx                    ;eg save size of transient in paragraphs

        SUB     AX,DX                           ; max seg addr - # para's needed for transient
        MOV     [TRNSEG],AX                     ;  = seg addr to load the transient at.

AX holds the PSP's PDB_block_len field, used here as the segment just past the end of the shell's block ("max seg addr" in the comment), and DX the transient size in paragraphs (16 bytes), so the transient ends exactly at the end of the block. INIT shrinks its own block to the resident size with SETBLOCK (INT 21h function 4Ah) and, if the old and new places do not overlap, copies the transient up to TRNSEG (backwards); if they overlap, it reads it from disk with LOADCOM instead (INIT.ASM lines 930-996). The init code becomes free memory. While the shell waits for a command, memory looks like this. The segment numbers and sizes are from the lab image (Module 0) as reported by the MCB walker of Module 2, Exercise 2.1, with the default CONFIG.SYS:

Diagram
 low addresses                                              high addresses
 +-----------+------------------+-------------+---------------------------+
 | DOS, IO,  | COMMAND resident | environment | TPA (free for programs)   |
 | drivers,  | PSP + CODERES +  | block       |            +--------------+
 | buffers   | part of DATARES  | (own arena) |            | transient    |
 |           |                  |             |            | at TRNSEG    |
 +-----------+------------------+-------------+------------+--------------+
  MCB 0BA1    MCB 108B           MCB 11F4     ^ a program loads here and
  owner 8     164h paragraphs    0Ah paras      may grow over the transient
              = 5,696 bytes      = 160 bytes    (28,020 bytes = 6D8h paragraphs)

(Exercise 3.1 asks you to read the segment sizes from the linker map and to explain why the resident block is smaller than the resident code and data in the map.)

The resident part: handlers, EXEC and reload#

SETVECT points three interrupt vectors at resident code:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.8 – SETVECT installs the INT 22h, 23h and 24h handlers (COMMAND2.ASM lines 544-556)Source ↗
SETVECT:                                ; Set useful vectors
        MOV     DX,OFFSET RESGROUP:LODCOM
        MOV     AX,(SET_INTERRUPT_VECTOR SHL 8) OR 22H
        MOV     WORD PTR DS:[PDB_EXIT],DX
        MOV     WORD PTR DS:[PDB_EXIT+2],DS
        INT     int_command
        MOV     DX,OFFSET RESGROUP:CONTC
        INC     AL
        INT     int_command
        MOV     DX,OFFSET RESGROUP:DSKERR
        INC     AL
        INT     int_command
        return

INT 22h, the terminate address where DOS continues when a program ends, is LODCOM. INT 23h, the Ctrl-C handler, is CONTC (3.8). INT 24h, the critical error handler, is DSKERR, which prints the error and then "Abort", ", Retry", ", Ignore", ", Fail" and "?", but only the choices DOS allows for this error (RUCODE.ASM lines 357-379, RESMSG.EQU lines 8-12). These handlers must be resident because they run while any program is running.

The resident part also performs the EXEC. The transient prepares everything, frees its own memory and jumps into the resident:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.9 – EXECUTE frees the transient's memory and jumps to the resident EXEC (excerpt) (TMISC1.ASM lines 318-352)Source ↗
EXECUTE:
NeoExecute:
        invoke  IOSET
        invoke  SETSTDINOFF                     ;AN026; turn off critical error on STDIN
        invoke  SETSTDOUTOFF                    ;AN026; turn off critical error on STDOUT
        MOV     ES,[TRAN_TPA]
        MOV     AH,DEALLOC
        INT     int_command                     ; Now running in "free" space
        MOV     ES,[RESSEG]
ASSUME  ES:RESGROUP
        INC     [EXTCOM]                        ; Indicate external command
        MOV     [RESTDIR],0                     ; Since USERDIR1 is in transient, insure
                                                ;  this flag value for re-entry to COMMAND
        MOV     DI,FCB
        MOV     SI,DI
        MOV     CX,052H                         ; moving (100h-5Ch)/2 = 80h-2Eh
        REP     MOVSW                           ; Transfer parameters to resident header
        MOV     DX,OFFSET TRANGROUP:EXECPATH
        MOV     BX,OFFSET RESGROUP:EXEC_BLOCK
        MOV     AX,EXEC SHL 8
⋮
;
; we are now running in free space.  anything we do from here on may get
; trashed.  Move the stack (also in free space) to allocated space because
; since EXEC restores the stack, somebody may trash what is on the stack.
;
        MOV     CX,ES
        MOV     SS,CX
        MOV     SP,OFFSET RESGROUP:RSTACK
        JMP     [EXEC_ADDR]                     ; Jmp to the EXEC in the resident

After DEALLOC (function 49h) the transient is executing in free memory, which is safe only because nothing allocates memory before the EXEC, and the stack is moved into the resident first. REP MOVSW copies the command tail and two pre-parsed FCBs from the transient's scratch area (offsets 5Ch-FFh) to the resident's PSP, where the EXEC parameter block points (3.7). Then:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.10 – the resident issues the EXEC, collects the exit code and goes to LODCOM (COMMAND1.ASM lines 455-474)Source ↗
EXT_EXEC:
        push    dx                              ;AN000; save the command name offset
        INT     int_command                     ; Do the EXEC
        pop     dx                              ;AN000; restore the command name offset
        JC      EXEC_ERR                        ; EXEC failed
;
; The exec has completed.  Retrieve the exit code.
;
EXEC_WAIT:
        push    cs                              ;AC000; get resident segment
        pop     ds                              ;AC000;     into DS
        MOV     AH,WAITPROCESS                  ;AC000; Get errorlevel
        INT     int_command                     ; Get the return code
        MOV     [RETCODE],AX
;
; We need to test to see if we can reload the transient.  THe external command
; may have overwritten part of the transient.
;
NOEXEC:
        JMP     LODCOM

When the child ends, DOS returns to the instruction after the INT, because EXEC stored the caller's return address as the child's terminate address (EXEC.ASM lines 746-755). Function 4Dh fetches the exit code into RETCODE, and LODCOM checks whether the program overwrote the transient: it recomputes a checksum of the transient and, if it differs from the value saved at initialisation, reads the transient back from the file named by COMSPEC. Study case 3.B follows this path.

A permanent shell also installs INT 2Eh (INIT.ASM lines 862-864), a back door through which a program can make the top-level shell execute a command line without loading a second COMMAND.COM:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.11 – INT 2Eh copies a command line into the shell's PSP and runs it (COMMAND2.ASM lines 186-203)Source ↗
INT_2E:                                 ; Magic command executer
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING,ES:NOTHING,SS:NOTHING
        POP     WORD PTR [INT_2E_RET]
        POP     WORD PTR [INT_2E_RET+2] ;Get return address
        POP     AX                      ;Chuck flags
        PUSH    CS
        POP     ES
        MOV     DI,80H
        MOV     CX,64
        REP     MOVSW
        MOV     AH,GET_CURRENT_PDB
        INT     int_command             ; Get user's header
        MOV     [SAVE_PDB],BX
        MOV     AH,SET_CURRENT_PDB
        MOV     BX,CS
        INT     int_command             ; Current process is me
        MOV     [SINGLECOM],81H
        MOV     [EXTCOM],1              ; Make sure this case forced

The handler copies 128 bytes from DS:SI (a count byte, the text and a carriage return) to its own PSP at 80h, makes itself the current process (function 50h) and sets SINGLECOM, so the normal loop runs one command and returns through RET_2E, which reports 0 for internal commands (lines 167-184). There is one INT_2E_RET save area, so the code is not re-entrant. INT 2Eh is usually described as undocumented; Ralf Brown's Interrupt List gives the calling convention this code implements.

Why /bin/sh needs none of this#

sh is an ordinary executable: its code pages are mapped read-only from /bin/sh and shared by every sh process, its data is private and copy-on-write after fork (Module 2). Running a program creates a new process with its own address space while the shell sleeps in wait; under memory pressure the kernel pages out what is least used and reads it back on demand. The kernel provides, generally and transparently, what COMMAND.COM implements by hand for one program.

MS-DOS 4.00 COMMAND.COM FreeBSD 15.1 sh
Memory while a program runs resident part only; transient may be overwritten whole shell mapped; pages may be evicted
Detecting damage checksum of transient code and data (CHKSUM) not needed: separate address spaces
Recovery re-read the transient from the COMSPEC file demand paging from /bin/sh
Who issues the run call resident code, after the transient frees itself the shell's child, after fork/vfork
Callbacks from the kernel INT 22h, 23h, 24h vectors signals (SIGCHLD, SIGINT, …)
Command for another program INT 2Eh, or EXEC COMMAND /C system(3): fork and exec sh -c (system.c lines 63-107)

3.3 The main loop: prompt, read, parse, dispatch#

COMMAND.COM: one line at a time#

The transient's recycle point is TCOMMAND in TCODE.ASM ("Nothing is known here", lines 111-135); every command and every error ends there. Each pass resets segments and stack, restores the standard handles, deletes finished pipe files and decides where the next command comes from, in priority order: a pipeline in progress, a FOR loop, a batch file, a /C command, and only then the keyboard (lines 255-341).

The prompt comes from the PROMPT variable; each $x code is looked up in PROMPT_TABLE, so $P$G calls build_dir_for_prompt and PRINT_G (TDATA.ASM lines 255-269, TCMD2A.ASM lines 105-160). The line is read with one DOS call:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.12 – reading a command line with INT 21h function 0Ah (TCODE.ASM lines 350-367)Source ↗
REGCOM:
        MOV     AX,(ServerCall SHL 8) + 9
        INT     21h
        MOV     AX,(ServerCall SHL 8) + 8
        MOV     DL,1
        INT     21h

        PUSH    CS
        POP     DS                              ; Need local segment to point to buffer
        MOV     DX,OFFSET TRANGROUP:UCOMBUF
        MOV     AH,STD_CON_STRING_INPUT
        INT     int_command                     ; Get a command
        MOV     CL,[UCOMBUF]
        XOR     CH,CH
        ADD     CX,3
        MOV     SI,OFFSET TRANGROUP:UCOMBUF
        MOV     DI,OFFSET TRANGROUP:COMBUF
        REP     MOVSB                           ; Transfer it to the cooked buffer

Function 0Ah does all the line editing (echo, Backspace, the F1-F3 template keys) and returns on Enter. Byte 0 of the buffer is the maximum length (COMBUFLEN = 128, COMEQU.ASM line 13), byte 1 receives the count. The raw buffer UCOMBUF is copied to COMBUF because the next steps edit the text in place: PRESCAN removes redirections and detects pipes (3.4, 3.5), parseline splits the words into an argv[]-like array, and the code builds the tail at 80h and FCBs at 5Ch and 6Ch as a program expects them in its PSP (TCODE.ASM lines 380-508). A command name without a drive letter is looked up in the internal command table:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.13 – COMTAB, the internal command table (excerpt) (TDATA.ASM lines 280-351)Source ↗
; Table for internal command names
COMTAB  DB      3,"DIR",fSwitchAllowed+fCheckDrive
        DW      OFFSET TRANGROUP:CATALOG        ; In TCMD1.ASM
        DB      4,"CALL",fSwitchAllowed
        DW      OFFSET TRANGROUP:$CALL          ; In TBATCH2.ASM
⋮
        DB      2,"CD",fSwitchAllowed+fCheckDrive    ;AC018; P3903
        DW      OFFSET TRANGROUP:$CHDIR         ; In TENV.ASM
        DB      5,"CHDIR",fSwitchAllowed+fCheckDrive ;AC018; P3903
        DW      OFFSET TRANGROUP:$CHDIR         ; In TENV.ASM
⋮
        DB      8,"TRUENAME",fSwitchAllowed+fCheckDrive  ;AN000; P3903 changed
        DW      OFFSET TRANGROUP:TRUENAME       ;AN000;
        DB      0                               ; Terminate command table

Each entry is a length byte, the name, a flag byte (fSwitchAllowed, fCheckDrive) and the handler's offset; a zero length ends the table. fndcom scans it linearly:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.14 – fndcom scans COMTAB (TMISC1.ASM lines 174-197)Source ↗
    mov     DI, OFFSET TRANGROUP:COMTAB
    XOR     CX,CX

findcom:
    mov     SI, offset TRANGROUP:IDLEN+1        ; pointer to command argument
    mov     CL, [DI]                            ; load length of internal command
    inc     di                                  ; advance past length
    jcxz    externalj                           ; if it's zero, we're out of internals
    cmp     CL, IDLEN                           ; that of the command argument
    jnz     abcd                                ; lengths not equal ==> strings not eq
    MOV     PathPos,CX                          ; store length of command
    repz    cmpsb

abcd:
    lahf                                        ; save the good ol' flags
    add     DI, CX                              ; skip over remaining internal, if any
    mov     AL, BYTE PTR [DI]                   ; load drive-check indicator byte (DCIB)
    mov     [CHKDRV], AL                        ; save command flag byte in chkdrv
    inc     DI                                  ; increment DI (OK, OK, I'll stop)
    mov     BX, WORD PTR [DI]                   ; load internal command address
    inc     DI                                  ; skip over the puppy
    inc     DI
    sahf                                        ; remember those flags?
    jnz     findcom                             ; well, if all the cmps worked...

On a match the shell applies redirection (ioset), checks drives and switches, and call BX runs the handler inside the transient; Cmd_done then returns to TCOMMAND (lines 198-251). Otherwise path_search looks for name.??? (built by strip, PATH2.ASM lines 334-344, unless the user typed an extension) with FIND FIRST/NEXT (functions 4Eh/4Fh) and ranks matches .COM over .EXE over .BAT (PATH2.ASM lines 85-108), first in the current directory, then in each ;-separated element of PATH (PATH1.ASM lines 244-261). A .COM or .EXE goes to EXECUTE (Listing 3.9), a .BAT to BatCom (3.6). Nothing is cached: every external command costs a directory search per PATH element until a match is found.

sh: parse a whole command into a tree, then evaluate it#

sh separates reading, parsing and evaluating:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.15 – cmdloop: parse one command, evaluate it, repeat (main.c lines 197-230)Source ↗
        for (;;) {
                if (pendingsig)
                        dotrap();
⋮
                n = parsecmd(inter);
                /* showtree(n); DEBUG */
                if (n == NEOF) {
                        if (!top || numeof >= 50)
                                break;
                        if (!stoppedjobs()) {
                                if (!Iflag)
                                        break;
                                out2fmt_flush("\nUse \"exit\" to leave shell.\n");
                        }
                        numeof++;
                } else if (n != NULL && nflag == 0) {
                        job_warning = (job_warning == 2) ? 1 : 0;
                        numeof = 0;
                        evaltree(n, 0);
                }
                popstackmark(&smark);
                setstackmark(&smark);
                if (evalskip != 0) {
                        if (evalskip == SKIPRETURN)
                                evalskip = 0;
                        break;
                }
        }

parsecmd() is a recursive-descent parser. It returns a tree of nodes whose types are declared in a small description file that mknodes turns into C at build time:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.16 – node types for simple commands and pipelines (nodetypes lines 54-62)Source ↗
NCMD ncmd                       # a simple command
        type      int
        args      nodeptr               # the arguments
        redirect  nodeptr               # list of file redirections

NPIPE npipe                     # a pipeline
        type      int
        backgnd   int                   # set to run pipeline in background
        cmdlist   nodelist              # the commands in the pipeline

list() handles ;, & and newlines, andor() handles && and ||, and pipeline() collects commands separated by |:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.17 – pipeline() builds an NPIPE node with a list of commands (parser.c lines 374-396)Source ↗
        n1 = command();
        if (readtoken() == TPIPE) {
                pipenode = (union node *)stalloc(sizeof (struct npipe));
                pipenode->type = NPIPE;
                pipenode->npipe.backgnd = 0;
                lp = (struct nodelist *)stalloc(sizeof (struct nodelist));
                pipenode->npipe.cmdlist = lp;
                lp->n = n1;
                do {
                        prev = lp;
                        lp = (struct nodelist *)stalloc(sizeof (struct nodelist));
                        checkkwd = CHKNL | CHKKWD | CHKALIAS;
                        t = readtoken();
                        tokpushback++;
                        if (t == TNOT)
                                lp->n = pipeline();
                        else
                                lp->n = command();
                        prev->next = lp;
                } while (readtoken() == TPIPE);
                lp->next = NULL;
                n1 = pipenode;
        }

ls | sort > out.txt thus becomes an NPIPE node listing two NCMD nodes, the second carrying an NTO redirection for out.txt; nothing has been opened yet. evaltree() walks the tree with a switch on node types (eval.c lines 182-301). For a simple command, evalcommand() expands the words and calls find_command(), which remembers where commands were found in a hash table of 31 buckets (exec.c lines 72-85):

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.18 – find_command: hash table first, then builtins, then PATH (exec.c lines 357-386)Source ↗
        /* If name contains a slash, don't use the hash table */
        if (strchr(name, '/') != NULL) {
                entry->cmdtype = CMDNORMAL;
                entry->u.index = 0;
                entry->special = 0;
                return;
        }

        cd = 0;

        /* If name is in the table, we're done */
        if ((cmdp = cmdlookup(name, 0)) != NULL) {
                if (cmdp->cmdtype == CMDFUNCTION && act & DO_NOFUNC)
                        cmdp = NULL;
                else
                        goto success;
        }

        /* Check for builtin next */
        if ((i = find_builtin(name, &spec)) >= 0) {
                INTOFF;
                cmdp = cmdlookup(name, 1);
                if (cmdp->cmdtype == CMDFUNCTION)
                        cmdp = &loc_cmd;
                cmdp->cmdtype = CMDBUILTIN;
                cmdp->param.index = i;
                cmdp->special = spec;
                INTON;
                goto success;
        }

Builtins come from a table generated from builtins.def (lines 49-91) by mkbuiltins (lines 57-69). It has COMTAB's shape (length byte, then a flags-and-index byte, then the name), and find_builtin() scans it just like fndcom. Otherwise find_command stat()s each PATH candidate and caches the index of the directory that matched (lines 388-442); hash -r or assigning PATH (changepath()) empties the cache. Then evalcommand decides whether to create a process:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.19 – evalcommand forks only for external commands (and some special cases) (eval.c lines 973-996)Source ↗
        /* Fork off a child process if necessary. */
        if (((cmdentry.cmdtype == CMDNORMAL || cmdentry.cmdtype == CMDUNKNOWN)
            && ((flags & EV_EXIT) == 0 || have_traps()))
         || ((flags & EV_BACKCMD) != 0
            && (cmdentry.cmdtype != CMDBUILTIN ||
                 !safe_builtin(cmdentry.u.index, argc, argv)))) {
                jp = makejob(cmd, 1);
                mode = FORK_FG;
                if (flags & EV_BACKCMD) {
                        mode = FORK_NOJOB;
                        if (pipe(pip) < 0)
                                error("Pipe call failed: %s", strerror(errno));
                }
                if (cmdentry.cmdtype == CMDNORMAL &&
                    cmd->ncmd.redirect == NULL &&
                    varlist.count == 0 &&
                    (mode == FORK_FG || mode == FORK_NOJOB) &&
                    !disvforkset() && !iflag && !mflag) {
                        vforkexecshell(jp, argv, environment(), path,
                            cmdentry.u.index, flags & EV_BACKCMD ? pip : NULL);
                        goto parent;
                }
                if (forkshell(jp, cmd, mode) != 0)
                        goto parent;    /* at end of routine */

Builtins and functions run in the shell process. An external command gets a child, created with vfork() in the simple non-interactive case (no redirections, no assignments, no job control) and with fork() otherwise. The child applies redirections, exports prefix assignments and execs:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.20 – the child applies redirections and execs the program (eval.c lines 1135-1145)Source ↗
        } else {
#ifdef DEBUG
                trputs("normal command:  ");  trargs(argv);
#endif
                redirect(cmd->ncmd.redirect, 0);
                for (i = 0; i < varlist.count; i++)
                        setvareq(varlist.args[i], VEXPORT|VSTACK);
                envp = environment();
                shellexec(argv, envp, path, cmdentry.u.index);
                /*NOTREACHED*/
        }

shellexec() tries execve() on the PATH candidates, starting at the cached index, and maps failures to exit status 127 ("not found") or 126 (exec.c lines 104-133). The parent calls waitforjob(), which blocks in wait3() (jobs.c lines 1171-1180) and returns the value of $?.

Step MS-DOS 4.00 COMMAND.COM FreeBSD 15.1 sh
Prompt PROMPT, $ codes PS1, \ codes (getprompt() in parser.c)
Read INT 21h 0Ah, one line of at most 128 bytes, editing by DOS read(2) of up to BUFSIZ bytes; libedit when interactive
Parse PRESCAN strips `< > >> in place;parseline` splits words
Internal lookup linear scan of COMTAB hash table, then builtincmd[]
External lookup FIND FIRST/NEXT per PATH entry, every time stat along PATH once, then cached
Run transient frees itself, resident does EXEC (4Bh) fork/vfork, child execves
Wait EXEC returns when the child ends; 4Dh gets the code wait3 in dowait(); status to $?

3.4 Redirection#

Both systems give a program three standard handles or descriptors: 0 (input), 1 (output) and 2 (errors). Redirection means making 0 or 1 refer to a file before the program starts, and putting things back afterwards. Module 2 described the structures: each DOS PSP has a 20-entry Job File Table (JFT, PDB_JFN_Table in PDB.INC lines 8-22) whose bytes index the system-wide System File Table (SFT); each FreeBSD process has a descriptor table pointing to shared struct files.

COMMAND.COM: editing its own Job File Table#

PRESCAN finds <, > and >>, stores the file names (RE_INSTR, RE_OUTSTR, with RE_OUT_APP for >>) and deletes them from the line (TMISC1.ASM lines 456-537). IOSET applies them just before an internal handler runs or a program is EXECed, except while a pipe or an IF is active (TMISC2.ASM lines 184-212):

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.21 – TESTDOREIN: open the file, then move its SFT index into slot 0 (TMISC2.ASM lines 214-238)Source ↗
TESTDOREIN:

ASSUME  DS:RESGROUP

        CMP     [RE_INSTR],0
        retz
        PUSH    DS
        PUSH    CS
        POP     DS
        MOV     DX,OFFSET tranGROUP:RE_INSTR
        MOV     AX,(OPEN SHL 8)
        MOV     BX,AX
        INT     int_command
        POP     DS
        JC      REDIRERR
        MOV     BX,AX
        MOV     AL,0FFH
;
; Mega sleaze!! We move the SFN from the new handle spot into the old stdin
; spot.  We invalidate the new JFN we got.
;
        XCHG    AL,[BX.PDB_JFN_Table]
        MOV     DS:[PDB_JFN_Table],AL

        return

The comment calls this "mega sleaze". DOS has dup-like calls (45h XDUP, 46h XDUP2), but the shell instead opens the file (getting, say, handle 5) and exchanges bytes in its own PSP: JFT slot 5 becomes 0FFh (unused) and slot 0 receives the file's SFT index. The console's index is not lost, because IO_SAVE has held slots 0 and 1 since initialisation (INIT.ASM lines 871-872). Output is the same after CREAT (3Ch), or after OPEN and a seek to the end for >>, where the code even backs up over a trailing Ctrl-Z (lines 280-360). A child EXECed now receives a copy of this JFT (Module 2), so its handles 0 and 1 are the files. Afterwards, HEADFIX restores the shell's table:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.22 – HEADFIX restores handles 0 and 1 and closes everything else (COMMAND2.ASM lines 345-369)Source ↗
HEADFIX:
        CALL    SETVECT
        XOR     BX,BX                   ; Clean up header
        MOV     CX,[IO_SAVE]
        MOV     DX,WORD PTR DS:[PDB_JFN_Table]
        CMP     CL,DL
        JZ      CHK1                    ; Stdin matches
        MOV     AH,CLOSE
        INT     int_command
        MOV     DS:[PDB_JFN_Table],CL   ; Restore stdin
CHK1:
        INC     BX
        CMP     CH,DH                   ; Stdout matches
        JZ      CHKOTHERHAND
        MOV     AH,CLOSE
        INT     int_command
        MOV     DS:[PDB_JFN_Table+1],CH ; Restore stdout
CHKOTHERHAND:
        ADD     BX,4                    ; Skip 2,3,4
        MOV     CX,FilPerProc - 5       ; Already done 0,1,2,3,4
CLOSELOOP:
        MOV     AH,CLOSE
        INT     int_command
        INC     BX
        LOOP    CLOSELOOP

If a slot differs from IO_SAVE, CLOSE (3Eh) drops the file and the saved index is written back. Handles 5 to 19 (FilPerProc is 20) are closed unconditionally. HEADFIX runs through LODCOM1 and at every TCOMMAND (CALL [HEADCALL]), so the restore follows every command, internal or external.

sh: dup2 and a stack of saved descriptors#

In sh, redirections are nodes (NTO, NFROM, NAPPEND, …, nodetypes lines 112-138). openredirect() opens the file and moves it onto the target with dup2:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.23 – openredirect: open, then dup2 onto the target descriptor (excerpt) (redir.c lines 205-243)Source ↗
        case NCLOBBER:
                fname = redir->nfile.expfname;
                if ((f = open(fname, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0666)) < 0)
                        error("cannot create %s: %s", fname, strerror(errno));
                break;
        case NAPPEND:
                fname = redir->nfile.expfname;
                if ((f = open(fname, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_APPEND, 0666)) < 0)
                        error("cannot create %s: %s", fname, strerror(errno));
                break;
⋮
        if (f != fd) {
                if (dup2(f, fd) == -1) {
                        e = errno;
                        close(f);
                        error("%d: %s", fd, strerror(e));
                }
                close(f);
        }

For an external command that is all: redirect(..., 0) runs in the child after fork (Listing 3.20), so the shell's own descriptors are never touched. A builtin runs in the shell, so redirect() with REDIR_PUSH first saves each descriptor it will replace:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.24 – redirect: save the old descriptor with F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC before replacing it (redir.c lines 128-155)Source ↗
        for (n = redir ; n ; n = n->nfile.next) {
                fd = n->nfile.fd;
                if (fd == 0)
                        fd0_redirected = 1;
                if ((n->nfile.type == NTOFD || n->nfile.type == NFROMFD) &&
                    n->ndup.dupfd == fd)
                        continue; /* redirect from/to same file descriptor */

                if ((flags & REDIR_PUSH) && sv->renamed[fd] == EMPTY) {
                        INTOFF;
                        if ((i = fcntl(fd, F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC, 10)) == -1) {
                                switch (errno) {
                                case EBADF:
                                        i = CLOSED;
                                        break;
                                default:
                                        INTON;
                                        error("%d: %s", fd, strerror(errno));
                                        break;
                                }
                        }
                        sv->renamed[fd] = i;
                        INTON;
                }
                openredirect(n, memory);
                INTON;
                INTOFF;
        }

fcntl(fd, F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC, 10) returns the lowest free descriptor of at least 10, marked close-on-exec so that later programs do not inherit it. The saved numbers live in a struct redirtab, and these form a stack (redirlist), so nested redirections unwind in order; popredir() dup2s the saved descriptors back and closes the copies (redir.c lines 303-330).

MS-DOS 4.00 COMMAND.COM FreeBSD 15.1 sh
Parsed by PRESCAN, text deleted from the line parser, nfile nodes on the command
Handles 0 (<) and 1 (>, >>) only any of 0-9, plus >&, <>, here-documents
Mechanism swap SFT index bytes in the shell's own JFT open + dup2
External command shell's table changed before EXEC; child inherits a copy done in the child after fork
Builtin / internal same JFT swap old descriptor saved with F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC
Undo HEADFIX compares with IO_SAVE; closes 5-19 popredir() from the redirtab stack
Append seek to end, overwrite a trailing Ctrl-Z O_APPEND

3.5 Pipes#

A pipe connects the standard output of one command to the standard input of the next. Under Unix it is a kernel object, a bounded buffer with a read end and a write end, and both programs run at once. MS-DOS 4.00 has no such object and runs one program at a time, so COMMAND.COM simulates a | b with files: run a with output to a temporary file, then run b with input from it.

COMMAND.COM: two temporary files in the root directory#

When PRESCAN sees | it sets PIPEFLAG, pushes the echo state, and finally copies the cooked line into PIPESTR in the resident data, where it survives while programs run (TMISC1.ASM lines 539-615). The file names are templates:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.25 – the pipe file name templates and the pipe state (RDATA.ASM lines 523-542)Source ↗
;--- 2.x data for piping
;
;  All the "_" are substituted later, the one before the : is substituted
; by the current drive, and the others by the CreateTemp call with the
; unique file name. Note that the first 0 is the first char of the pipe
; name. -MU
;
;--- Order dependant, do not change

Pipe1           db      "_:/"
Pipe1T          db      0
                db      "_______.___",0
Pipe2           db      "_:/"
Pipe2T          db      0
                db      "_______.___",0

PIPEPTR         DW      ?
PIPESTR         DB      129 DUP(?)
INPIPEPTR       DW      OFFSET ResGroup:PIPE1
OUTPIPEPTR      DW      OFFSET ResGroup:PIPE2

PIPEPROCSTRT puts the current drive letter in front of each :/, cuts the name after it, and asks DOS to create a uniquely named file in that directory (INT 21h function 5Ah, CreateTempFile):

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.26 – PIPEPROCSTRT creates both pipe files in the root of the current drive (TPIPE.ASM lines 171-200)Source ↗
PIPEPROCSTRT:
ASSUME  DS:TRANGROUP,ES:TRANGROUP
        MOV     DS,[RESSEG]
ASSUME  DS:RESGROUP
        INC     [PIPEFILES]                     ; Flag that the pipe files exist
        MOV     AH,Get_Default_Drive            ; Get current drive
        INT     int_command
        ADD     AL,capital_A
        MOV     [PIPE2],AL                      ; Make pipe files in root of def drv
        MOV     BX,OFFSET RESGROUP:PIPE1
        MOV     [BX],AL
        xor     ah,ah                           ; nul terminate path names
        mov     [Pipe1T],ah
        mov     [Pipe2T],ah
        MOV     DX,BX
        XOR     CX,CX
        mov     ah,CreateTempFile               ; the CreateTemp call
        INT     int_command
        JC      PIPEERR                         ; Couldn't create
        MOV     BX,AX
        MOV     AH,CLOSE                        ; Don't proliferate handles
        INT     int_command

        MOV     DX,OFFSET RESGROUP:PIPE2
        mov     ah,createTempFile               ; the CreateTemp call
        INT     int_command
        JC      PIPEERR
        MOV     BX,AX
        MOV     AH,CLOSE
        INT     int_command

Two details matter because later DOS versions differ. The files go in the root of the current drive; nothing in the 4.00 COMMAND sources consults a TEMP variable (a case-insensitive search for TEMP finds only CreateTempFile and words like "attempt"). And the files are closed at once and reopened by name in each stage, so a write-protected disk (or a full root directory) makes the pipe fail with "Intermediate file error during pipe" (COMMAND.SKL line 187, via PIPEERR, TPIPE.ASM lines 154-169).

The main loop calls PIPEPROC first whenever PIPEFLAG is set (TCODE.ASM lines 261-263). Each stage reads handle 0 from the file the previous stage wrote, writes handle 1 to the other file, and runs through the normal path; at the end PIPEDEL deletes both files with function 41h (TPIPE.ASM lines 130-146). Study case 3.A walks through the steps. The consequences are direct: stages run strictly one after another, the whole intermediate output must fit on the disk, and a producer that never ends hangs the pipeline with a growing file. In exchange, the mechanism needs nothing from the kernel but files and works with every program that uses standard input and output.

sh: pipe(2) and concurrent processes#

sh turns an NPIPE node into processes in evalpipe():

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.27 – evalpipe creates one pipe per '|' and forks every stage (eval.c lines 575-606)Source ↗
        for (lp = n->npipe.cmdlist ; lp ; lp = lp->next) {
                prehash(lp->n);
                pip[1] = -1;
                if (lp->next) {
                        if (pipe(pip) < 0) {
                                if (prevfd >= 0)
                                        close(prevfd);
                                error("Pipe call failed: %s", strerror(errno));
                        }
                }
                if (forkshell(jp, lp->n, n->npipe.backgnd) == 0) {
                        INTON;
                        if (prevfd > 0) {
                                dup2(prevfd, 0);
                                close(prevfd);
                        }
                        if (pip[1] >= 0) {
                                if (!(prevfd >= 0 && pip[0] == 0))
                                        close(pip[0]);
                                if (pip[1] != 1) {
                                        dup2(pip[1], 1);
                                        close(pip[1]);
                                }
                        }
                        evaltree(lp->n, EV_EXIT);
                }
                if (prevfd >= 0)
                        close(prevfd);
                prevfd = pip[0];
                if (pip[1] != -1)
                        close(pip[1]);
        }

For each command but the last, pipe() creates a pipe (pip[0] read end, pip[1] write end). Each child dup2s the previous read end onto 0 and the new write end onto 1, closes the originals and evaluates its command with EV_EXIT, so a simple command execs directly. The parent closes the ends it no longer needs and starts the next stage without waiting; only then does it call waitforjob(). The closing matters: a reader sees end-of-file only when every write descriptor is closed, including stray copies in the parent.

In FreeBSD 15.1 the C library's pipe() simply calls pipe2(fildes, 0) (pipe.c lines 39-44), and kern_pipe() allocates a pipepair and two descriptors (sys_pipe.c lines 480-528). A new pipe normally gets PIPE_SIZE = 16 KiB of buffer and may grow to BIG_PIPE_SIZE = 64 KiB, or get one page when pipe memory is scarce (pipe.h lines 28-38, sys_pipe.c lines 58-74). When the buffer is full the writer sleeps in pipe_write() ("pipewr"); when it is empty the reader sleeps in pipe_read() ("piperd"). This blocking makes a pipeline self-regulating: the producer runs at the consumer's speed and memory use stays bounded. If the reader is gone, pipe_write() returns EPIPE (lines 1157-1165) and the generic write path sends SIGPIPE (sys_generic.c lines 570-579), which is how yes | head -1 ends.

MS-DOS 4.00 COMMAND.COM FreeBSD 15.1 sh
Channel two temporary files X:\ + unique name (5Ah) kernel pipe, 16 KiB buffer, up to 64 KiB
Execution sequential concurrent, one process per stage
Flow control none needed writer and reader sleep and wake
Size limit free disk space none (data streams through the buffer)
End of data end of the temporary file all write ends closed; SIGPIPE for a writer without reader
Cleanup PIPEDEL; after Ctrl-C at the next TCOMMAND (lines 203-207) pipe freed at the last close
Pipeline status RETCODE of the last external program status of the last command

3.6 Batch files and shell scripts#

How COMMAND.COM runs a batch file#

When path_search finds a .BAT file, BatCom allocates a batch segment describing the running batch file and stores its segment in BATCH (TBATCH.ASM lines 680-932):

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.28 – the batch segment structure (COMEQU.ASM lines 176-185)Source ↗
BatchSegment    struc
BatType         DB      BatchType       ; signature
Batechoflag     DB      0               ; G state of echo
Batlast         DW      0               ; G segment of last batch file
Batforptr       DW      0               ; G segment for FOR command
Batforflag      DB      0               ; G state of FOR
BatSeek         DD      ?               ; lseek position of next char
BatParm         DW      10 dup (?)      ; pointers to parameters
BatFile         DB      ?               ; beginning of batch file name
BatchSegment    ends

The file name and the arguments follow the fixed part; BatParm points to the first ten (%0-%9). The key field is BatSeek, a 32-bit byte offset into the file. The file is not kept open: for every line, ReadBat calls PromptBat, which calls BatOpen:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.29 – BatOpen reopens the batch file by name and seeks to BatSeek (TBATCH2.ASM lines 712-735)Source ↗
Procedure   BatOpen,NEAR

ASSUME  DS:RESGROUP,ES:TRANGROUP

        PUSH    DS
        MOV     DS,[BATCH]
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING

        MOV     DX,BatFile
        MOV     AX,OPEN SHL 8
        INT     int_command                     ; Open the batch file
        JC      SETERRDL
        MOV     DX,WORD PTR DS:[BatSeek]
        MOV     CX,WORD PTR DS:[BatSeek+2]
        POP     DS
ASSUME  DS:RESGROUP

        MOV     [BATHAND],AX
        MOV     BX,AX
        MOV     AX,LSEEK SHL 8                  ; Go to the right spot
        INT     int_command
        MOV     BatBufPos,-1                    ; nuke batch buffer position

        return

GetBatByt reads through a 32-byte buffer (BatLen, COMEQU.ASM line 14) and adds one to BatSeek for every byte consumed ( TBATCH2.ASM lines 68-131); Ctrl-Z or end of file ends batch mode. At the end of each line the file is closed again:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.30 – at the end of a line: set the length, eat the LF, BATCLOSE (TBATCH.ASM lines 302-317)Source ↗
SAVBATBYT:
        STOSB
        CMP     AL,0DH                          ; End of line found?
        JNZ     RDBAT                           ; no, go for more
;
; We have read in an entire line.  Decide whether we should echo the command
; line or not.
;

Found_EOL:
        SUB     DI,OFFSET TRANGROUP:COMBUF+3
        MOV     AX,DI                           ; remember that we've not counted the CR
        MOV     ES:[COMBUF+1],AL                ; Set length of line
        invoke  GetBatByt                       ; Eat linefeed
        invoke  BATCLOSE
        CMP     SUPPRESS, NO_ECHO               ;G

This open-seek-read-close cycle per line explains several behaviours. If the floppy holding the batch file is removed, PromptBat asks "Insert disk with batch file" ( lines 84-135). No handle is held while a batch command runs. And if the file is edited while it runs, the next line is read from the new contents at the old byte offset, possibly from the middle of a line (Exercise 3.3).

The rest of the language is built from the same pieces:

  • Parameters. RDBAT replaces %0-%9 by arguments, %% by %, and %NAME% by an environment value (lines 362-533); SHIFT slides the ten pointers down (TBATCH2.ASM lines 446-495).
  • Echo. A leading @ suppresses echo of one line (lines 250-253); ECHOFLAG is a bit-stack pushed and popped around pipes and batch files (RDATA.ASM lines 462-466).
  • GOTO. Lines starting with : are skipped; GOTO rescans the file from byte 0 (Study case 3.C).
  • IF. ERRORLEVEL n (true when the last exit code is at least n: CMP AH,BL / JAE), EXIST file and a==b, optionally with NOT; a true condition runs the rest of the line (TBATCH2.ASM lines 175-435).
  • FOR. FOR %v IN (list) DO command runs the command once per item, expanding wildcards with FIND FIRST/NEXT; only one FOR may be active ("FOR cannot be nested", TFOR.ASM lines 327-332).
  • CALL. Starting a batch file from a batch file replaces the current one (BatchOff frees its segment). CALL exists in 4.00 ($CALL; the revision log dates it to 3.30, COMMAND1.ASM lines 112-119); it keeps the old segment and links the new one to it through Batlast.

There are no shell variables, no structured loops, no functions and no arithmetic.

How sh runs a script#

A script is read by the same code as the terminal: preadfd() refills a buffer of BUFSIZ bytes with read(2) on a descriptor that stays open for the whole script:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.31 – preadfd: refill the input buffer with read(2) (interactive editing elided) (input.c lines 124-155)Source ↗
static int
preadfd(void)
{
        int nr;
        parsenextc = parsefile->buf;

retry:
⋮
                nr = read(parsefile->fd, parsefile->buf, BUFSIZ);

BUFSIZ is 1024 (stdio.h line 209). Parsing is incremental by complete commands, not lines: cmdloop parses one list, evaluates it, and parses the next. A while loop or a function definition is parsed completely into a tree (NWHILE, NFOR, NIF, NCASE, NDEFUN, nodetypes lines 75-104) and runs from memory, never re-reading the file. sh also has what batch files lack: unexported variables, unlimited positional parameters, arithmetic, case, functions with local variables, and here-documents, fed to the command through a pipe that the shell fills itself if the text fits (redir.c lines 253-295).

MS-DOS 4.00 batch file FreeBSD 15.1 sh script
File access reopen, seek to BatSeek, 32-byte reads, close after each line one open descriptor, 1024-byte reads
Unit of parsing one line one complete command (may span lines)
Loops GOTO rescans from byte 0; one-level FOR while/until/for run from a tree
Parameters %0-%9, SHIFT $0, $1, …, ${10}, shift, $#, $@
Variables environment only (%NAME%) shell variables; export puts them in the environment
Conditions IF ERRORLEVEL (>= n), EXIST, == any command's status; test builtin
Subroutines CALL another batch file functions; . to source a file
File edited while running next line read from the new text at the old offset text already parsed is unaffected; later reads continue at the descriptor's offset; a file replaced by mv is not seen

3.7 The environment#

In both systems the environment is a list of NAME=value strings that a program receives from its parent.

The DOS environment block#

An MS-DOS environment is a memory block of its own (with an arena header, Module 2) holding NUL-terminated NAME=value strings, ended by an empty string. Its segment is at offset 2Ch of the PSP (PDB_environ, PDB.INC line 27). COMMAND.COM edits its own block in place. SET NAME=value checks for exactly one =, deletes any old entry, upper-cases the name and appends the string; SET NAME= only deletes; SET alone prints the block (TENV.ASM lines 102-158). PATH and PROMPT are ordinary entries edited by internal commands of the same names, and setting COMSPEC also updates the resident copy used by LOADCOM (lines 143-237). When the block is full, STORE_CHAR frees the transient, tries to grow the environment by one paragraph with SETBLOCK, and reallocates the transient:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.32 – STORE_CHAR grows the environment, up to 32 KB, unless it would hit the transient (TENV.ASM lines 549-570)Source ↗
        invoke  FREE_TPA
        POP     BX
        ADD     BX,2                            ; Recover true environment size

        CMP     BX, 8000H                       ; Don't let environment grow > 32K
        JB      ENVSIZ_OK
BAD_ENV_SIZE:                                   ;AN056;
        STC
        JMP     ENVNOSET
ENVSIZ_OK:

        MOV     CL,4
        SHR     BX,CL                           ; Convert back to paragraphs
        INC     BX                              ; Try to grow environment by one para
        MOV     CX,ES                           ;AN056; Get environment segment
        ADD     CX,BX                           ;AN056; Add in size of environment
        ADD     CX,020H                         ;AN056; Add in some TPA
        MOV     AX,CS                           ;AN056; Get the transient segment
        CMP     CX,AX                           ;AN056; Are we hitting the transient?
        JNB     BAD_ENV_SIZE                    ;AN056; Yes - don't do it!!!
        MOV     AH,SETBLOCK
        INT     int_command

Growth fails with "Out of environment space" at 32 KB, when it would reach the transient, or when SETBLOCK fails because the next block belongs to someone else (for example a resident program loaded later). Hence /E:n: without it the size is ENVSML = 160 bytes, or more if the inherited strings need it (INIT.ASM lines 19-23 and lines 1075-1103).

To run a program, COMMAND.COM passes its environment segment in the EXEC parameter block:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.33 – the EXEC parameter block starts with the environment segment (RDATA.ASM lines 544-554)Source ↗
EXEC_BLOCK      LABEL   BYTE                    ; The data block for EXEC calls
ENVIRSEG        DW      ?
COM_PTR         LABEL   DWORD
                DW      80H                     ; Point at unformatted parameters
                DW      ?
COM_FCB1        LABEL   DWORD
                DW      5CH
                DW      ?
COM_FCB2        LABEL   DWORD
                DW      6CH
                DW      ?

DOS does not give the child that block. EXEC measures it (at most 32 KB), allocates a block just large enough, copies the strings and appends a word 1 and the program name passed to EXEC (EXEC.ASM lines 241-278). The child's copy has no spare room and is independent: a program, even a secondary COMMAND.COM, can change its own copy, but the change vanishes when it exits. Only the shell that owns a block can change it for its future children, which is why SET must be internal.

sh variables and environ#

sh keeps variables in a hash table of 39 chains (var.c lines 66-67). At startup initvar() imports every string of environ with the VEXPORT flag (lines 179-183); new variables are exported only after export. The environment for a program is built on demand as an array of pointers for execve:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.34 – environment() builds envp from the exported variables (var.c lines 543-564)Source ↗
environment(void)
{
        int nenv;
        struct var **vpp;
        struct var *vp;
        char **env, **ep;

        nenv = 0;
        for (vpp = vartab ; vpp < vartab + VTABSIZE ; vpp++) {
                for (vp = *vpp ; vp ; vp = vp->next)
                        if ((vp->flags & (VEXPORT|VUNSET)) == VEXPORT)
                                nenv++;
        }
        ep = env = stalloc((nenv + 1) * sizeof *env);
        for (vpp = vartab ; vpp < vartab + VTABSIZE ; vpp++) {
                for (vp = *vpp ; vp ; vp = vp->next)
                        if ((vp->flags & (VEXPORT|VUNSET)) == VEXPORT)
                                *ep++ = vp->text;
        }
        *ep = NULL;
        return env;
}

Assignments before a command name, as in LANG=C sort file, are exported only in the child (setvareq(..., VEXPORT|VSTACK) in Listing 3.20). execve copies the strings into the new image (Module 2), so, as in DOS, the child's environment is a copy.

MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Representation one block of NAME=value\0 strings plus a final \0 char **environ, pointers to strings
Kept by the shell as its own block, edited in place, grown with SETBLOCK hash table of struct var; envp built per exec
Size limit at most 32 KB, set by /E:n, must not collide with other blocks ARG_MAX for arguments and environment (syslimits.h)
Names upper-cased by SET case-sensitive
Passed to the child EXEC copies the block and appends the program name execve copies envp
Unexported variables none yes

3.8 Ctrl-C, signals and job control#

Ctrl-C in MS-DOS: INT 23h#

MS-DOS checks for Ctrl-C (or Ctrl-Break) during console I/O, and during other calls only when BREAK=ON (CNTCFLAG, DISP.ASM lines 377-381), and then issues INT 23h. By default the vector points at COMMAND.COM's resident CONTC (Listing 3.8):

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.35 – CONTC, the default INT 23h handler (excerpt) (COMMAND1.ASM lines 482-622)Source ↗
CONTC   PROC    FAR
        ASSUME  CS:ResGroup,DS:NOTHING,ES:NOTHING,SS:NOTHING
        test    InitFlag,initINIT               ; in initialization?
        jz      NotAtInit                       ; no
        test    InitFlag,initSpecial            ; doing special stuff?
        jz      CmdIRet                         ; no, ignore ^C
        jmp     resgroup:init_contc_specialcase ; Yes, go handle it
CmdIret:
        iret                                    ; yes, ignore the ^C
⋮
        TEST    Batch,-1
        JZ      CONTCTERM
        OR      AX,AX
        JNZ     Contcterm
        invoke  SavHand
        invoke  ASKEND                          ; See if user wants to terminate batch
;
; If the carry flag is clear, we do NOT free up the batch file
;
        JNC     ContBatch
⋮
; If we are doing an internal command, go through the reload process.  If we
; are doing an external, let DOS abort the process.  In both cases, we are
; now done with the ^C processing.
;
        AND     InitFlag,NOT initCtrlC
        CMP     [EXTCOM],AL
        JNZ     DODAB                           ; Internal ^C
        JMP     LODCOM1
DODAB:
        STC                                     ; Tell DOS to abort
        RET                                     ; Leave flags on stack

The handler ignores Ctrl-C during initialisation (except at the date and time prompts), resets the disks (function 0Dh), and inside a batch file asks "Terminate batch job (Y/N)?" (ASKEND, RUCODE.ASM lines 104-115), freeing the batch and FOR segments on "Y". It always switches off IF, FOR and pipe processing. Then, if an external program was running (EXTCOM non-zero), STC and RET with the flags left on the stack tell DOS to abort it, and DOS continues at the terminate address EXEC recorded, just after the INT 21h in EXT_EXEC (EXEC.ASM lines 746-755), from where EXEC_WAIT goes on to LODCOM; for an internal command the handler jumps straight to LODCOM1. There is one foreground program and no way to suspend it.

Signals, process groups and job control in sh#

In FreeBSD the terminal driver turns VINTR (normally Ctrl-C) into SIGINT, VQUIT into SIGQUIT and VSUSP (Ctrl-Z) into SIGTSTP (tty_ttydisc.c lines 1115-1133), and sends the signal to the terminal's foreground process group (tty.c lines 1531-1552). A process group is a set of processes, usually one pipeline, signalled together. Job control is the shell's management of these groups; it is on by default in an interactive shell (mflag = iflag, options.c lines 100-101). forkshell() puts each job in its own group and gives a foreground job the terminal:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.36 – forkshell: a new process group per job, and the terminal for foreground jobs (jobs.c lines 919-936)Source ↗
                if (wasroot && mode != FORK_NOJOB && mflag) {
                        if (jp == NULL || jp->nprocs == 0)
                                pgrp = getpid();
                        else
                                pgrp = jp->ps[0].pid;
                        if (setpgid(0, pgrp) == 0 && mode == FORK_FG &&
                            ttyfd >= 0) {
                                /*
                                 * Each process in a pipeline must have the tty
                                 * pgrp set before running its code.
                                 * Only for pipelines of three or more processes
                                 * could this be reduced to two calls.
                                 */
                                if (tcsetpgrp(ttyfd, pgrp) < 0)
                                        error("tcsetpgrp failed, errno=%d", errno);
                        }
                        setsignal(SIGTSTP);
                        setsignal(SIGTTOU);

The parent also calls setpgid (lines 973-979), so the group exists whichever runs first. Only the foreground group receives Ctrl-C, so the shell is not interrupted. Ctrl-Z stops the job; wait3 with WUNTRACED reports it and waitforjob() takes the terminal back (lines 1094-1101). fg gives the terminal to the job's group and sends SIGCONT to the whole group with kill(-pgid, SIGCONT); bg sends SIGCONT only (lines 241-300). The shell's own SIGINT handler, onsig(), aborts the current command line or, inside an INTOFF/INTON critical region, only records the signal (trap.c lines 371-392); these regions play the role of InitFlag in CONTC.

MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Ctrl-C delivered as INT 23h, in the running program's context SIGINT to the foreground process group
Default effect CONTC: ask about the batch file, abort the program terminate the process unless caught or ignored
Shell protects itself by InitFlag bits own process group; INTOFF/INTON
Suspend and resume not possible Ctrl-Z, fg, bg, jobs
Background programs none &, $!, wait

Study cases#

Study case 3.A: dir | sort > out.txt end to end#

Goal: follow one command line through each shell, naming every routine and system call. On FreeBSD we use ls | sort > out.txt.

MS-DOS 4.00 (current drive C:, SORT.EXE found through PATH):

  1. Read and prescan. Function 0Ah fills the buffer (Listing 3.12). PRESCAN stores out.txt in RE_OUTSTR and drops it from the line; at | it pushes the echo state and sets PIPEFLAG; it copies dir | sort into PIPESTR, and DOCOM1 jumps to PIPEPROCSTRT.
  2. Create the files. Two calls to function 5Ah create two empty files in C:\ (Listing 3.26).
  3. Stage 1. FIRSTPIPE copies dir into COMBUF; the code below creates the output file as handle 1:
MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.37 – each stage: CREAT the output pipe file, swap names; the last stage takes the > file instead (TPIPE.ASM lines 272-301)Source ↗
IsPipe2:
        MOV     BYTE PTR ES:[DI-1],0DH
        DEC     CX
        MOV     [COMBUF+1],CL
        DEC     SI
        MOV     [PIPEPTR],SI                    ; On to next pipe element
        MOV     DX,[OUTPIPEPTR]
        PUSH    CX
        XOR     CX,CX
        MOV     AX,(CREAT SHL 8)
        INT     int_command
        POP     CX
        JC      PIPEERRJ                        ; Lost the file
        MOV     BX,AX
        MOV     AL,0FFH
        XCHG    AL,[BX.PDB_JFN_Table]
        MOV     DS:[PDB_JFN_Table+1],AL
        XCHG    DX,[INPIPEPTR]                  ; Swap for next element of pipe
        MOV     [OUTPIPEPTR],DX
        JMP     SHORT PIPECOM

LASTPIPE:
        MOV     [COMBUF+1],CL
        DEC     SI
        MOV     [PIPEPTR],SI                    ; Point at the CR (anything not '|' will do)
        CALL    TESTDOREOUT                     ; Set up the redirection if specified
PIPECOM:
        PUSH    CS
        POP     DS
        JMP     NOPIPEPROC                      ; Process the pipe element
  1. Run DIR. fndcom finds DIR in COMTAB; ioset does nothing because PIPEFLAG is set; CATALOG writes to handle 1, the second temporary file (PIPE2, named by OUTPIPEPTR). Back at TCOMMAND, HEADFIX (Listing 3.22) closes handle 1 and restores the console. PIPEFLAG is still set, so the files stay.
  2. Stage 2. GETCOM enters PIPEPROC, which opens the file just written (INPIPEPTR) and moves it into slot 0. sort ends at the carriage return, so LASTPIPE calls TESTDOREOUT, which CREATs out.txt into slot 1.
  3. Run SORT. path_search finds SORT.EXE; EXECUTE and EXT_EXEC run it (Listing 3.9, Listing 3.10). SORT reads the whole pipe file, sorts in memory, writes out.txt and exits; LODCOM restores the handles and checks the transient (Study case 3.B).
  4. Clean up. PIPEPROC finds no further |; PIPEEND calls PIPEDEL, which UNLINKs both files (41h) and pops the echo state.

FreeBSD 15.1:

  1. Parse. parsecmd() returns NPIPE{ NCMD(ls), NCMD(sort) }, the second with an NTO node (Listing 3.17).
  2. Stage 1. evalpipe() (Listing 3.27) calls pipe(), getting for example descriptors 3 (read) and 4 (write), and forks. The child joins the job's process group, does dup2(4, 1), closes 3 and 4, and runs ls with EV_EXIT, so evalcommand does not fork again and shellexec() calls execve. The parent closes 4 and keeps 3.
  3. Stage 2. The second child does dup2(3, 0) and closes 3, opens out.txt with O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC and dup2s it onto 1 (Listing 3.23), and execs sort. The parent closes 3.
  4. Run. Both programs run at once. If sort falls behind and the buffer fills, ls sleeps:
FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.38 – pipe_write: no space left, so sleep on "pipewr" until the reader drains the buffer (sys_pipe.c lines 1338-1359)Source ↗
                        /*
                         * don't block on non-blocking I/O
                         */
                        if (fp->f_flag & FNONBLOCK) {
                                error = EAGAIN;
                                break;
                        }

                        /*
                         * We have no more space and have something to offer,
                         * wake up select/poll.
                         */
                        pipeselwakeup(wpipe);

                        wpipe->pipe_state |= PIPE_WANTW;
                        pipeunlock(wpipe);
                        error = msleep(wpipe, PIPE_MTX(rpipe),
                            PRIBIO | PCATCH, "pipewr", 0);
                        pipelock(wpipe, false);
                        if (error != 0)
                                break;
                        continue;
  1. End of data. When ls exits, the last write descriptor closes (the parent closed its copy), sort's read returns 0, and sort writes its output and exits.
  2. Wait. waitforjob() collects both children with wait3(); the status is sort's.

To watch it: truss -f -o trace.txt sh -c 'ls | sort > out.txt', then look for pipe2, two forks, dup2, the openat of out.txt and two execves, and note which process makes each call.

What to notice:

  • COMMAND.COM does all the plumbing in its own JFT, one stage at a time, with the data on disk in between. sh does the plumbing in each child; the data never touches the disk.
  • > applies only to the last stage because LASTPIPE calls TESTDOREOUT; in sh the parser attached it to the second NCMD.
  • DIR runs inside COMMAND.COM yet takes part in the pipe through handle 1; in sh every stage of a pipeline, even a builtin, runs in a forked child.
MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Intermediate storage two files in C:\ (5Ah) kernel buffer, 16 KiB
Processes one at a time; DIR inside the shell two children, concurrent
Plumbing calls 5Ah, 3Ch, 3Dh, JFT byte swaps, 3Eh pipe2, fork, dup2, close, openat
out.txt opened by the shell, before SORT runs the second child, before execve
Synchronisation sequential, none needed sleep and wakeup in pipe_write/pipe_read
Cleanup PIPEDEL, two UNLINKs last close frees the pipe

Discussion questions:

  1. SORT must read all its input before writing anything. Does the temporary-file design cost SORT much? Which program loses more from it, SORT or MORE?
  2. Why must the parent close its copy of the write end in evalpipe()? What happens to sort if line 605 is removed?
  3. Why does COMMAND.COM need two files even for one |, and how many does a | b | c | d use?

Study case 3.B: the transient-part reload and its checksum#

Goal: find out exactly what COMMAND.COM checks when a program ends, what it reloads, and what can go wrong.

After a program ends, LODCOM reallocates the largest free block and needs room for the transient plus 512 bytes (ADD AX,20H), otherwise "Memory allocation error" and, for a permanent shell, "Cannot load COMMAND, system halted" (lines 123-149). It places the transient at the top again (TRNSEG, lines 226-253) and continues:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.39 – LODCOM1: compare the checksum and reload until it matches (COMMAND2.ASM lines 270-287)Source ↗
        CMP     [SINGLECOM],-1
        JNZ     NOSNG
        JMP     FATALRET2               ; We have finished the single command
NOSNG:
        CALL    CHKSUM                  ; Check the transient
        CMP     DX,[SUM]
        JZ      HAVCOM                  ; Transient OK
BOGUS_COM:
        MOV     [LOADING],1             ; Flag DSKERR routine
        CALL    LOADCOM
CHKSAME:

        CALL    CHKSUM
        CMP     DX,[SUM]
        JZ      HAVCOM                  ; Same COMMAND
ALSO_BOGUS:
        CALL    WRONGCOM
        JMP     SHORT CHKSAME
MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.40 – CHKSUM: an end-around-carry sum of the transient's code and data (COMMAND2.ASM lines 526-542)Source ↗
CHKSUM:                                 ; Compute transient checksum
        PUSH    DS
        MOV     DS,[TRNSEG]
        MOV     SI,100H
        MOV     CX,OFFSET TRANGROUP:TranDataEnd  - 100H

CHECK_SUM:
        CLD
        SHR     CX,1
        XOR     DX,DX
CHK:
        LODSW
        ADD     DX,AX
        ADC     DX,0
        LOOP    CHK
        POP     DS
        return

Three details are worth noticing. The range runs from offset 100h to TranDataEnd: code and data that is mostly constant (a few message-control variables in TRANDATA are included), but not the variables in TRANSPACE, which change in normal use; those that matter are copied from the resident on every entry (TRANVARS, lines 298-304). ADC DX,0 adds each carry back in, making a 16-bit ones' complement sum, the family of the Internet checksum: cheap, and it detects most single-word changes, but not a word changed from 0000h to FFFFh (both count as zero in ones' complement) and not swapped words. And SUM is computed once, by INIT, right after the transient is moved into place (INIT.ASM lines 992-996).

If the sums differ, LOADCOM opens the COMSPEC file, seeks to TRANSTART and reads the transient (minus its 100h-byte scratch header) to TRNSEG:100h:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.41 – LOADCOM: open COMSPEC, seek to TRANSTART, read the transient, verify the size (excerpt) (COMMAND2.ASM lines 479-524)Source ↗
LOADCOM:                                ; Load in transient
        INC     BP                      ; Flag command read
        MOV     DX,OFFSET RESGROUP:COMSPEC
        MOV     AX,OPEN SHL 8
        INT     int_command             ; Open COMMAND.COM
        JNC     READCOM
⋮
READCOM:
        MOV     BX,AX                   ; Handle
        MOV     DX,OFFSET RESGROUP:TRANSTART
        XOR     CX,CX                   ; Seek loc
        MOV     AX,LSEEK SHL 8
        INT     int_command
        JC      WRONGCOM1
        MOV     CX,OFFSET TRANGROUP:TRANSPACEEND - 100H

        PUSH    DS
        MOV     DS,[TRNSEG]
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING
        MOV     DX,100H
        MOV     AH,READ
        INT     int_command
        POP     DS
ASSUME  DS:RESGROUP
WRONGCOM1:
        PUSHF
        PUSH    AX
        MOV     AH,CLOSE
        INT     int_command             ; Close COMMAND.COM
        POP     AX
        POPF
        JC      WRONGCOM                ; If error on READ
        CMP     AX,CX
        retz                            ; Size matched
WRONGCOM:
        MOV     DX,COMBAD               ;AC000;
        CALL    GETCOMDSK
        JMP     LOADCOM                 ; Try again

If the file cannot be opened on a removable drive, GETCOMDSK prints "Insert disk with %1 in drive %2" (with the COMSPEC path and drive) and waits for a key (lines 437-477); on a fixed disk it goes to HOPELESS, which prints "Invalid COMMAND.COM" and halts a permanent shell. A file of the wrong size, or one whose checksum still differs (ALSO_BOGUS), also gives "Invalid COMMAND.COM"; on a removable drive the shell then asks for the disk again, on a fixed disk it ends in HOPELESS as well: this catches a disk with a different DOS version.

FreeBSD needs none of this: nothing can overwrite a sleeping shell's memory, and evicted pages of /bin/sh are read back on demand. The kernel even prevents the file from changing underneath a running program: writing to an executable in use fails with ETXTBSY (vn_writechk()), whereas COMMAND.COM detects the problem after the fact.

What to notice:

  • The check costs one pass over the transient each time the resident regains control (after an external program, after Ctrl-C, or through INT 2Eh; an internal command returns straight to TCOMMAND without it), far cheaper on a 4.77 MHz 8088 than reading the transient from a floppy, which is the cost it avoids.
  • Programs that leave the top of memory alone never cause a reload.
MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
What can be lost transient code and data at the top of the TPA nothing; pages may be evicted, not overwritten
Detection CHKSUM vs SUM after every program not needed
Recovery LOADCOM reads the COMSPEC file page faults read /bin/sh
Protection of the file none; size and checksum checked after reading ETXTBSY while it is mapped as text

Discussion questions:

  1. Describe a .COM program that forces a reload and one that does not. What property decides it?
  2. Would an 8-bit sum or an XOR have done? What corruption would they miss, and does it matter here?
  3. A program runs COMMAND /C, and the secondary shell's COMSPEC names a floppy that has been removed. Which code path runs, and what does the user see?

Study case 3.C: batch interpretation vs script parsing#

Goal: see how each shell's reading strategy determines the cost of loops and the effect of editing a running file.

Example 3.C.1 – a polling loop as a batch file (COUNT.BAT)
@ECHO OFF
:LOOP
IF EXIST STOP.TXT GOTO END
ECHO tick >> LOG.TXT
GOTO LOOP
:END
Example 3.C.2 – the same loop as an sh script (count.sh)
#!/bin/sh
while [ ! -e stop.txt ]; do
    echo tick >> log.txt
done

In COMMAND.COM each pass executes three lines, and each line costs an open and a seek (Listing 3.29), a 32-byte read to look ahead for a : label, a seek back to the start of the line and a second read (TBATCH.ASM lines 230-267), and a close (Listing 3.30). GOTO remembers nothing about labels:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.42 – GOTO rewinds BatSeek to 0 and scans the file for the label (excerpt) (TBATCH2.ASM lines 568-617)Source ↗
GOTO:

assume  ds:trangroup,es:trangroup
        MOV     DS,[RESSEG]
ASSUME  DS:RESGROUP
        TEST    [BATCH],-1
        retz                                    ; If not in batch mode, a nop
        XOR     DX,DX
        PUSH    DS
        MOV     DS,Batch
        MOV     WORD PTR DS:[BatSeek],DX        ; Back to start
        MOV     WORD PTR DS:[BatSeek+2],DX      ; Back to start
        POP     DS

GotoOpen:
        invoke  promptBat
⋮
; At beginning of file.  Skip to first non-delimiter char
;
        CALL    SkipDelim
        JC      BadGoto
        CMP     AL,':'
        JZ      CHKLABEL

LABLKLP:                                        ; Look for the label
        CALL    GETBATBYT
        CMP     AL,0AH
        JNZ     LABLKTST
;
; At beginning of line.  Skip to first non-delimiter char
;
        CALL    SkipDelim
        JC      BadGoto
        CMP     AL,':'
        JZ      CHKLABEL

LABLKTST:
        TEST    [BATCH],-1
        JNZ     LABLKLP

Every GOTO rereads the file from byte 0 until a line starting with : matches, ignoring case (CHKLABEL, lines 630-691), so a jump to a label near the end of a long file reads the whole file on every iteration. The design keeps no state but BatSeek: it costs no memory and tolerates edits, but loops are slow.
