sh reads the four lines of while ... done before executing anything; parsecmd() returns one NWHILE node whose children are the test and the body, and evalloop() runs that tree repeatedly (eval.c lines 304-339). The file is not touched again until the loop ends. [ and echo are builtins (builtins.def), so the loop forks nothing; only >> is opened and closed, with the descriptor save and restore of Listing 3.24.

Now insert a line REM x at the top of each file while it runs:

  • COMMAND.COM reopens the file and seeks to the old BatSeek, which now points 7 bytes (REM x, CR, LF) earlier in the text, so it may execute the end of a line or a line twice. After the next GOTO, which restarts at byte 0, it is back in step.
  • sh keeps running the loop it already parsed. Text after done is read later from the descriptor's current offset in the modified file.

What to notice:

  • A batch file is interpreted line by line from the file; an sh script is parsed into trees command by command and executed from memory.
  • GOTO, the only backward jump in the batch language, costs a scan from the start of the file.
MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
State between lines BatSeek and the batch segment open descriptor, buffer, parse tree
Cost of an iteration open/seek/read/close per line, plus a scan per GOTO evaluating an in-memory tree
Labels linear search every time not needed (structured loops)
Effect of an edit next line read at the old offset of the new text running command unaffected

Discussion questions:

  1. Count the INT 21h calls COMMAND.COM makes for one iteration of COUNT.BAT. Which dominate on a floppy?
  2. Why might the designers have preferred reopening the file for each line? Consider handles, removable disks and CALL.
  3. What does parsing a whole while loop before running it imply for a script piped into sh over a slow connection?

Study case 3.D: a builtin vs an external command, and why cd must be a builtin#

Goal: decide from the kernel's data structures which commands must run inside the shell.

In FreeBSD the current directory is per-process state, kept in a struct pwd reached from the process's pwddesc:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.43 – the per-process directory state (filedesc.h lines 94-108)Source ↗
struct pwd {
        u_int           pwd_refcount;
        struct  vnode   *pwd_cdir;      /* current directory */
        struct  vnode   *pwd_rdir;      /* root directory */
        struct  vnode   *pwd_jdir;      /* jail root directory */
        struct  vnode   *pwd_adir;      /* abi root directory */
};
typedef SMR_POINTER(struct pwd *) smrpwd_t;

struct pwddesc {
        struct mtx      pd_lock;        /* protects members of this struct */
        smrpwd_t        pd_pwd;         /* directories */
        u_int           pd_refcount;
        u_short         pd_cmask;       /* mask for file creation */
};

chdir(2) changes only the caller's pwd (kern_chdir() ends in pwd_chdir(), vfs_syscalls.c lines 946-965), and fork gives the child a copy (pdcopy, kern_fork.c lines 469-475). An external cd would change its own directory and exit, leaving the shell where it was, so cd is a builtin whose cdlogical() or cdphysical() calls chdir() in the shell process (cd.c lines 172-242). FreeBSD still installs a /usr/bin/cd: a script, linked under several builtin names (Makefile lines 4-17), that runs the builtin in a new shell:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 3.44 – /usr/bin/cd and friends: run the builtin of the same name (generic.sh lines 1-3)Source ↗
#!/bin/sh
# This file is in the public domain.
builtin ${0##*/} ${1+"$@"}

/usr/bin/cd /tmp succeeds and changes nothing for its caller, which makes the point well.

MS-DOS 4.00 is different. The PSP has no current-directory field:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 3.45 – the PSP: handles and environment, but no current directory (PDB.INC lines 10-27)Source ↗
Process_data_block  STRUC
PDB_Exit_Call       DW      ?           ; INT int_abort system terminate
PDB_block_len       DW      ?           ; size of execution block
                    DB      ?
PDB_CPM_Call        DB  5 DUP (?)       ; ancient call to system
PDB_Exit            DD      ?           ; pointer to exit routine
PDB_Ctrl_C          DD      ?           ; pointer to ^C routine
PDB_Fatal_abort     DD      ?           ; pointer to fatal error
;----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----;
;            C  A  V  E  A  T     P  R  O  G  R  A  M  M  E  R             ;
;                                                                          ;
PDB_Parent_PID      DW      ?           ; PID of parent (terminate PID)
PDB_JFN_Table       DB  FilPerProc DUP (?)
                                        ; indices into system table
;                                                                          ;
;            C  A  V  E  A  T     P  R  O  G  R  A  M  M  E  R             ;
;----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----;
PDB_environ         DW      ?           ; seg addr of environment

Each drive's current directory lives in the system-wide Current Directory Structure (CDS). $CHDIR, the handler of INT 21h function 3Bh, validates the path and copies it into the drive's CDS (PATH.ASM lines 214-295); nothing is per process. A program that calls function 3Bh changes the directory for everyone, and the change outlives it, so an external CD.COM would work. COMMAND.COM's CD (TENV2.ASM lines 98-155) is internal for speed and convenience. The shell even guards against the global directory: if an internal command that changed directories is interrupted, it restores the user's directory from USERDIR1 (TCODE.ASM lines 182-200). In DOS the command that must be internal is SET, because the environment is per process (3.7); GOTO, SHIFT, IF, FOR, CALL and EXIT must be internal because they act on COMMAND.COM's own state.

What to notice:

  • "Must be built in" is a statement about where the kernel keeps state: per-process state can only be changed by code running in that process.
  • DOS keeps the current directory and drive globally, so any program can change them.
Command MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
cd internal by choice; an external one would work must be builtin: cwd is per process
set / assignment must be internal: environment is per process must be builtin
umask not applicable must be builtin (pd_cmask in pwddesc)
echo internal (no program to load) builtin, for speed

Discussion questions:

  1. Sketch a DOS program UP.COM that does cd ... Why does it work, and what does that say about isolation between DOS programs?
  2. The current drive is also global. Where does GETCOM read it on every command, and why must it?
  3. Name a FreeBSD builtin that need not be one, and explain why sh implements it anyway.

Homework#

Exercise 3.1: Exit codes, IF ERRORLEVEL and the size of the transient#

Difficulty: basic. Estimated time: 2 h.

Tasks:

  1. Trace an exit code from INT 21h function 4Ch in a child, through EXEC_WAIT (Listing 3.10), to IFERLEV in TBATCH2.ASM. Name every variable the value passes through.
  2. Explain from the code why IF ERRORLEVEL 0 is always true, and why a batch file must test IF ERRORLEVEL 2 before IF ERRORLEVEL 1. Give the sh equivalent of IF ERRORLEVEL 2 GOTO X.
  3. Using COMMAND.MAP from your Module 0 build tree (build/dos4/SRC/CMD/COMMAND/COMMAND.MAP; the link step uses /map, see COMMAND.LNK), find the sizes of the resident and transient parts and compute how many bytes a large program gains by overwriting the transient part. Then compare the resident size in the map with the size of COMMAND.COM's memory block that the MCB walker of Module 2 (Exercise 2.1) or MEM /DEBUG reports, and explain the difference from INIT.ASM.

Deliverables: a one-page trace with permalinks for every step, the answer to task 2, and the sizes (or the explanation) for task 3.

Hints: RETCODE is a word but IFERLEV compares only one byte. SetSize is in COMMAND2.ASM.

Exercise 3.2: Watching the pipe files#

Difficulty: basic. Estimated time: 1.5 h.

Tasks (MS-DOS lab VM):

  1. With C: as the current drive, run DIR C:\ | SORT. Find the two temporary files in the output and explain, with PIPEPROCSTRT and CreateTempFile, why they appear and why their sizes are what DIR shows.
  2. Run DIR C:\ again and explain why the files are gone (PIPEDEL).
  3. Make a write-protected floppy the current drive (or use a full disk image) and run DIR | SORT. Record every message and match each one to the code that prints it (INT 24h handler and PIPEERR).

Deliverables: screen captures or transcripts, and an explanation citing the source lines.

Hints: DOS, not COMMAND.COM, chooses the names.

Exercise 3.3: Editing a running batch file#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 2.5 h.

Tasks:

  1. In the MS-DOS VM, write SELF.BAT that echoes three numbered lines, then runs COPY NEW.BAT SELF.BAT, then echoes three more lines. Prepare NEW.BAT so that its first lines are longer or shorter than those of SELF.BAT. Predict, from BatSeek, BatOpen and GetBatByt, exactly which text COMMAND.COM reads after the COPY, then run it.
  2. Repeat with ECHO OFF and with @ prefixes, and explain any difference in what is displayed.
  3. In FreeBSD, write the equivalent self.sh using cp new.sh self.sh and, in a second experiment, cp new.sh tmp.sh && mv tmp.sh self.sh. Explain both results from preadfd(), the open descriptor and the difference between overwriting a file and replacing a directory entry.

Deliverables: the four scripts, transcripts, and a prediction-versus-result table with explanations.

Hints: count the CR and LF bytes. cp truncates and rewrites the existing file; mv replaces the name.

Exercise 3.4: A .COM program that shows its PSP#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

Tasks:

  1. Complete the template below with nasm so that SHOWPSP.COM prints its command tail (offset 80h) between brackets, then every environment string on its own line, then the program path that follows the environment. Write all output with INT 21h function 40h to handle 1.
  2. Run SHOWPSP a b, SHOWPSP a > OUT.TXT, SHOWPSP < SHOWPSP.COM and SHOWPSP a | SORT, and explain what appears in the command tail in each case (PRESCAN, the tail copied in EXECUTE).
  3. Run SET X=1 before and inside COMMAND /C SHOWPSP and explain what the child sees (3.7, EXEC.ASM).
Template 3.4 – skeleton for SHOWPSP.COM (nasm syntax; build with nasm -f bin -o SHOWPSP.COM showpsp.asm)
        org     100h            ; a .COM program starts at PSP:0100h
start:
        mov     si, 81h         ; command tail text
        mov     cl, [80h]       ; command tail length
        xor     ch, ch
        ; TODO: print "[", the CX bytes at DS:SI, "]", CR LF  (AH=40h, BX=1)
        mov     es, [2Ch]       ; environment segment from the PSP
        xor     di, di
        ; TODO: loop over ASCIZ strings at ES:DI until an empty string
        ; TODO: skip the word after the final NUL and print the path
        mov     ax, 4C00h       ; exit with code 0
        int     21h

Deliverables: source, transcripts, explanations.

Hints: function 40h takes DS:DX, so set DS to the environment segment while printing those strings and restore it afterwards. DEBUG.COM can show the PSP of a program you load with DEBUG SHOWPSP.COM a b.

Exercise 3.5: A new builtin for FreeBSD sh#

Difficulty: advanced. Estimated time: 4 h.

Tasks (FreeBSD VM, /usr/src/bin/sh):

  1. Add a builtin pids that prints the shell's process ID, its parent's, its process group and the terminal's foreground process group (getpid, getppid, getpgrp, tcgetpgrp(0)). Add one line to builtins.def and a C function pidscmd(int argc, char **argv) to an existing source file such as miscbltin.c; mkbuiltins generates the table entry and the prototype.
  2. Build with make in /usr/src/bin/sh (use make -V .OBJDIR to find the binary) and run the new sh. Show that pids runs without a fork (truss -f), that pids | cat runs in a child, and compare the process groups printed in both cases with job control on and off (set +m).
  3. Explain each difference using evalcommand(), evalpipe() and forkshell().

Deliverables: a diff, transcripts and a half-page explanation.

Hints: use out1fmt() for output so that redirection and $(...) work; return 0 for success. Do not install the new shell as /bin/sh.

Exercise 3.6: Concurrency versus temporary files#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 2 h.

Tasks:

  1. In FreeBSD, run yes | head -n 3 and truss -f sh -c 'yes | head -n 3'. Find the write that fails in yes, the error, and the signal that ends it. Point to the kernel lines that produce them.
  2. Measure time sh -c 'yes | head -n 1000000 > /dev/null' and explain why memory use stays small.
  3. In MS-DOS, modify SHOWPSP (Exercise 3.4) into FOREVER.COM that writes a line in an endless loop, and run FOREVER | MORE. Describe what happens, why MORE never shows anything, and whether anything but Ctrl-C can stop the pipeline. Stop it with Ctrl-C and check whether the pipe files were deleted.

Deliverables: transcripts, the kernel citations, and a comparison table of the two behaviours.

Hints: pipe_write() returns EPIPE; the signal is raised in sys_generic.c. In DOS, think about what WRITE returns on a full disk and whether FOREVER checks it.

Exercise 3.7: Essay: how hardware shaped COMMAND.COM#

Difficulty: advanced. Estimated time: 3 h.

Write 1,200-1,500 words on which features of COMMAND.COM follow from its hardware and kernel (one task, 640 KB, floppy disks, no memory protection) and which would have been possible anyway. Cover at least the resident/transient split, temporary-file pipes, reopening batch files for every line, and the global current directory; for each, state what FreeBSD 15.1 sh does instead and which kernel feature makes it possible. Support every claim with a permalink.

Deliverables: the essay, with permalinks.

Hints: source comments are good evidence of intent, for example the header of COMMAND1.ASM and the long FOR comment in TFOR.ASM.

Further reading#

  • The FreeBSD sh(1) manual page, https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?query=sh&sektion=1&manpath=FreeBSD+15.1-RELEASE, and the index of builtins in builtin(1), https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?query=builtin&sektion=1&manpath=FreeBSD+15.1-RELEASE.
  • pipe(2), https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?query=pipe&sektion=2&manpath=FreeBSD+15.1-RELEASE.
  • Kenneth Almquist, "A Tour through Ash" (1989), shipped as bin/sh/TOUR; the file itself warns that the shell has changed since, but the structure it describes is still recognisable.
  • M. K. McKusick, G. V. Neville-Neil, R. N. M. Watson, The Design and Implementation of the FreeBSD Operating System, 2nd ed., Addison-Wesley, 2014: the chapters on process management (process groups, sessions, job control, signals) and on interprocess communication.
  • The MS-DOS Encyclopedia, Microsoft Press, 1988: the material on COMMAND.COM, batch files and the Program Segment Prefix.
  • Ralf Brown's Interrupt List, https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~ralf/files.html: INT 21h functions 0Ah, 4Bh, 5Ah and INT 2Eh.
  • Microsoft's MS-DOS repository and README, https://github.com/microsoft/MS-DOS, and the COMMAND sources used in this module: v4.0/src/CMD/COMMAND.
